summaries.example: Imagine a toy car that is stopped and then starts rolling. Before it moves, it is in one place. Later, it is in another. Philosophers ask: during the tiny moment when it starts, is it stopped, moving, or somehow both? One answer says change is smooth and can be described with time. Another says the changing car may need to be described as having opposite features during the change.
summaries.summary: Change is everywhere: objects move, temperatures shift, and things gain or lose features. The entry concentrates on temporal change, meaning change as time passes. It separates change from cause: something might change without a known cause, and a cause might prevent a change. It also explains that time and change are closely connected, while motion is change of place. Philosophers have offered different answers to a difficult question: how can one thing remain the same while having opposite features at different times? A consistent answer describes the features as belonging to the thing at different times. An inconsistent answer says that, during a transition, opposite descriptions may both be needed. Discussions of starting motion, Zeno’s arrow, changing objects, and the way we see moving things all put pressure on simple answers. The entry presents both approaches and concludes that the idea of inconsistency in change deserves serious attention.
key_ideas: Change can mean difference, but philosophers mainly study changes that happen through time.
Cause, time, and motion are connected to change, but they are not exactly the same thing.
Some philosophers have tried to show that change is impossible or only an illusion.
A major puzzle is how one thing can stay the same while having different features at different times.
Some philosophers argue that change may involve contradictions, especially when we think about motion.
The entry does not settle every puzzle, but it says the case for change involving inconsistency is stronger than it may first seem.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about change helps us understand ordinary experiences such as growing, moving, and starting or stopping. It also shows why everyday words can hide deep questions. The topic connects ideas about objects, time, motion, logic, and perception. Learning about the disagreement teaches us that a problem can remain open even when everyone agrees that change seems real.

important_terms.definition: A difference in something’s features. In this entry, the main focus is on a thing’s features changing as time passes.
A change in where something is. A rolling ball is an example of motion.
The idea that a thing stays the same thing even while some of its features change.
A statement that seems to say opposite things are true together, such as “the car is moving” and “the car is not moving.”

questions_to_think_about: When a ball begins rolling, is there one exact moment when it changes from stopped to moving?
Can something stay the same object while its color, place, or speed changes?
Is a moving picture really a set of still pictures, or is motion something more?
Could our minds help create the puzzling experience of things changing?

summaries.example: Consider a particle whose position is fixed before time 0 and then increases after time 0. If its position is described by a function with a sharp corner at 0, its speed may be clear on either side but undefined at the boundary. Assigning it one speed at exactly 0 can look arbitrary. One response is to say that the model is too rough and impose smoother functions. Another is to question whether a changing object can have a fully consistent description at the transition. Similar issues appear in motion: a cinematic view treats motion as occupying different positions at different times, while an intrinsic view seeks something about the object at the instant itself that makes it moving.
summaries.summary: The entry examines temporal change as alteration in a thing’s features and asks how such alteration can be logically and metaphysically understood. Change is not identical with cause, though a theory of causation may constrain acceptable accounts; nor is it simply time, although temporal change presupposes the passage of time in the framework adopted here. Motion is treated as change of place. Arguments by Parmenides, Zeno, and McTaggart attempt to deny change or show that it is unintelligible, but the entry finds their premises disputable or incomplete. The problem of the instant of change shows that no single answer follows without further assumptions about the functions and structures that describe a possible world. The central issue is consistency. If an object persists while its intrinsic properties alter, the indiscernibility of identicals appears to generate incompatible attributions. Time-slice theories, property-indexing, and event- or exemplification-based analyses offer different responses. In discussions of motion, Priest’s intrinsic account argues against a merely cinematic succession of states and links motion to contradiction, while critics can insist that change is essentially relational. A qualified continuity principle offers a route to describing some discontinuous but causal processes as inconsistent continuous functions. Finally, analyses of motion perception suggest that delayed and combined sensory information, together with object persistence, may help explain why experience represents changing stages as one enduring object. The conclusion is not that every issue is resolved, but that the connection between change and inconsistency is philosophically substantial.
key_ideas: Temporal change must be distinguished from cause, although causation may constrain how change is understood.
The instant of change is not one uniform problem: its solution depends on assumptions about possible worlds, functions, and metaphysical principles.
Persistence creates tension with the indiscernibility of identicals: if one object is identical across times, it appears to inherit incompatible properties.
Time-slice or perdurantist theories avoid some contradictions by treating things-at-times as fundamental, but they revise ordinary ideas of persistence.
Arguments for inconsistent motion challenge the cinematic view by asking what, at an instant, distinguishes motion from rest and how motion arises from point-instants.
The Leibniz Continuity Condition can support a qualified inconsistent account of continuous change, while the source also notes important logical and theoretical objections.
summaries.why_it_matters: The problem matters because it tests basic assumptions about objects, identity, time, logic, and scientific description. Classical mathematics can describe motion with functions, yet philosophical questions remain about what those descriptions mean at boundaries and instants. The debate also bears on continuity, causation, theories of persistence, and the interpretation of physical processes. The discussion of perception adds another level: even if the external world is consistently described, the experience of motion may combine information in a way that produces tension between distinct stages and one continuing object.

important_terms.definition: Change in a thing’s true descriptions, including changes in its relations to other things; it need not be a change in the thing’s intrinsic features.
A property belonging to a thing in itself, rather than a relation it has to other things.
A property involving a thing’s relation to something else, such as being someone’s sibling or being beside an object.
A theory in which contradictions can be true without making every statement true; it is relevant to proposals about inconsistent change.
The view that what exists fundamentally may be a thing at a particular time, with persistence built from time-slices.
The claim that what holds up to a limit also holds at that limit, with qualifications about which statements it applies to.
A description of motion as a succession of positions at different times, like connected frames in a film.
The proposal that a changing thing can have incompatible properties at a transition, rather than merely having them at separate times.

questions_to_think_about: Does a relation to nearby times adequately explain motion, or must motion be intrinsic to an object at an instant?
If a person is red at one time and not red at another, what exactly remains identical?
Are time-slices a genuine explanation of persistence or only a reformulation of the problem?
Does Zeno’s arrow argument expose a problem in the mathematical description of motion, or only a conceptual discomfort?
Could perceptual mechanisms that combine information from nearby times explain why motion seems to involve one enduring object?

summaries.example: Suppose a phone is on a desk and then is picked up. At the first time it is on the desk; later it is in your hand. It seems to be one phone throughout. But if “being on the desk” and “being in your hand” are opposite properties, how can the same thing have both? One solution adds time: the phone is on the desk at one time and in your hand at another. Another solution asks whether the change itself involves a short transition in which ordinary, non-contradictory descriptions are not enough.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what change is and how it can be possible. Its main subject is temporal change: a thing having different features as time passes. Change is related to cause, time, and motion, but none of these ideas simply means the same thing. For example, a thing might change without a known cause, while a cause might keep a thing from changing. Motion is a special kind of change involving place. Philosophers who deny change have argued that coming into or going out of existence, empty space, or the passage of time creates contradictions. The entry treats these arguments as important but not decisive. A harder puzzle concerns identity. If one object is the same at two times, it seems that it should have all the same properties; yet changing objects do not. Some theories solve this by treating properties as time-relative or by treating time-slices as basic. Other theories argue that a genuine transition cannot be described without inconsistency. The discussion of motion compares a “cinematic” picture, in which movement is a sequence of positions, with an intrinsic picture, in which something about the object at the instant makes it moving. The entry also considers whether perception joins nearby moments into an enduring moving object. Its overall conclusion is cautious: the idea that change involves inconsistency is not easily dismissed.
key_ideas: The entry studies temporal change, not every kind of difference.
A cause can produce change, but change does not always need a cause, and a cause can sometimes prevent change.
Some philosophers deny change by arguing that it leads to impossible ideas; the entry examines why those arguments may not work.
The puzzle of persistence asks how one object can remain identical while its features change.
One approach places different properties at different times. Another takes seriously the possibility that change itself is inconsistent.
The way people perceive moving objects may help explain why motion seems to involve both separate stages and one continuing thing.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic connects familiar events—starting, stopping, moving, and changing—with difficult questions about logic and reality. It helps explain why philosophers disagree even when they share the same everyday observations. It also shows how mathematics, theories of time, and studies of perception can approach one question from different directions. Understanding the debate encourages careful thinking about what words such as “same,” “now,” and “moving” really claim.

important_terms.definition: A difference in a thing’s features. The entry focuses especially on changes that happen as time passes.
Change in a thing’s location or position.
The feature that makes an object the same object at different times.
A property belonging to a thing itself, rather than to its relationships with other things.
A property described in relation to something else, such as being taller than another person.
A claim that puts incompatible descriptions together, such as saying something is both moving and not moving.
The view that a continuing object is made from different time-slices, or stages, that exist at particular times.

questions_to_think_about: When exactly does a stopped bicycle become a moving bicycle?
Does adding “at a certain time” solve the problem of incompatible properties?
Would a bicycle still be one object if we understood it as a series of time-slices?
Can a mathematical description of motion explain what motion really is?
Why might the brain represent flashing lights as one moving light?
